about: What a relay's `OK false` means. The host writes these prefixes and the client reads
them, and the two must agree — so both read this file and both fail when one of them stops matching it.
NIP-01 makes the prefix the machine-readable part and the rest of the reason a sentence for a person.
So this pins the prefixes and never the prose: a host is free to reword what it says and not free to
say it under a word the client cannot read.
`offer` is what the client answers with. `took` is a relay that has the note. `refused` is that note's
own verdict, for good — the mark moves past it and nothing offers it again. `unsettled` is the relay
talking about the account or about itself rather than about the note, which is the only reason to come
`blocked` is the one word here that reads against the common one. NIP-01 offers it for a note nobody
will ever take, and this network writes it for an account over its allowance — a door that opens again,
since a deletion request is exempt from the ceiling. So it is unsettled, and a kind a relay does not
keep is settled by that relay's own document instead.
A refusal the client cannot place is `unsettled`, because a host that says something new may be saying
it about itself. That is the safe default for an unknown word and the wrong one for a known word,
which is why every word the host can write is here.
`cases` are whole reasons, read as a client reads them: the prefix decides and nothing after it does.
